intro: Languages build words and sentences in different ways. Linguists sort them by how much one word can hold and how its pieces are joined — morphological typology. There are four classic types. Most languages mix them, so a type names a language's main tendency, not a box it fits exactly. The type decides what you must learn first, so every language of this course follows the path of its type.

types.name: Isolating (analytic)
types.summary: Words do not change their form. Grammar is carried by word order and by separate small words: particles, measure words, helper verbs. One word ≈ one piece of meaning.
types.learnFirst: word order, the small grammar words (particles, measure words), and — in tone languages — the tones; there are no endings and no tables to learn.

examples.analysis: wǒ ‘I’ · zuótiān ‘yesterday’ · chī ‘eat’ · le (particle: done) · sān ‘three’ · ge (measure word) · píngguǒ ‘apple’ — the past and the plural are not marked on any word.
tôi ‘I’ · ăn ‘eat’ · ba ‘three’ · quả (classifier for fruit) · táo ‘apple’ — the same building blocks as in Chinese.

types.languages: Mandarin and the other Chinese languages, Vietnamese, Thai, Yoruba; English leans strongly this way (I will have eaten).

types.name: Agglutinating
types.summary: Words are built by gluing endings (or prefixes) on one after another. Each piece has one meaning and keeps its shape, apart from sound rules such as vowel harmony. A long word is read piece by piece.
types.learnFirst: the pieces and their fixed order, vowel harmony, and the case endings that do the work of prepositions.

examples.analysis: ev ‘house’ + -ler (plural) + -imiz ‘our’ + -den ‘from’ — one meaning per piece, always in this order.

types.languages: Turkish, Finnish, Hungarian, Japanese, Korean, Swahili, Quechua.

types.name: Fusional (inflecting)
types.summary: Words change form too, but one ending carries several meanings at once (fused), the stem itself may change, and the endings differ from one word class to another — so they are learned in tables (paradigms), with gender and agreement.
types.learnFirst: gender and agreement, the most frequent tables (articles, pronouns, the present tense), and learning every noun with its gender and plural.

examples.tr: of the word, of the reason
examples.analysis: -ου says genitive + singular at once; there is no separate piece for each meaning, and other noun classes use other endings for the same job (της γυναίκας).
книг- ‘book’ + -ами = instrumental + plural in one ending.
the root k-t-b ‘writing’ is woven into vowel patterns inside the word — Semitic fusional morphology (also called introflexive).

types.languages: Greek, Latin, Russian, German, the Romance languages; Arabic and Hebrew, with roots and patterns inside the word.

types.name: Polysynthetic
types.summary: One verb can hold what other languages say with a whole sentence: the subject, the object, often a noun and adverbs are built into it.
types.learnFirst: the order of the pieces inside the verb, and the person markers for the subject and the object.

examples.analysis: tusaa- ‘hear’ + -tsiaq- ‘well’ + -junnaq- ‘be able’ + -nngit- ‘not’ + -tualuu- ‘very much’ + -junga ‘I’ — a whole sentence in one word (Inuktitut).
ni- ‘I’ + naca- ‘meat’ + qua ‘eat’ — the object noun is built into the verb (noun incorporation, Classical Nahuatl).

types.languages: Inuktitut and the other Inuit languages, Mohawk, Cherokee, Nahuatl, Chukchi, many languages of the Americas and Siberia.

spectrum: No language is pure. English is mostly analytic but keeps fused forms (went, children). German is fusional but builds compounds the agglutinating way (Gemüsesuppe = Gemüse + Suppe). Turkish is agglutinating with a few fused forms. Chinese builds compounds and has a few suffix-like particles. A language follows the path of its main type here; its other traits are taught as its peculiarities.
